title: Finland's ICEYE Bids €2B for Italian Rocket Maker Avio, Russian Tu-95 Bombers Land in Vietnam After Japan Airspace Breach, and Senators Reject Steam Catapults on Ford Carriers
subhead: Finnish satellite operator ICEYE launches a €2 billion cash bid for Italian rocket builder Avio as Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby warns NATO against excluding US arms suppliers; Russian Tu-95 bombers reach Da Nang after breaching Japanese airspace while a military plane crash in Siberia kills 19; and the Senate Armed Services chair calls reverting Ford-class carriers to steam catapults a non-starter.

sections.heading: Finland's ICEYE Bids €2B for Italy's Avio as Colby Warns NATO Allies Over Arms Procurement
sections.body:
Defense News, Breaking Defense, and Reuters — Finnish radar-satellite company ICEYE launched a €2 billion ($2.2 billion) cash offer for Italian rocket manufacturer Avio on Tuesday, seeking to build an integrated European space and defense group as European governments worry about heavy dependence on the United States for orbital launch and military space access (Defense News, Breaking Defense). Transatlantic industrial tensions surfaced simultaneously as Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby warned NATO allies against shutting US defense contractors out of European arms deals (Reuters via Google News Defense).

Friction over allied defense policy also spilled into public view after a European defense chief snapped back at a Pentagon official over US criticism regarding Ukraine (Wall Street Journal via Google News Defense). Meanwhile, Fortune reported that defense technology executives are pressing the Pentagon to overhaul its 'Industrial Age' acquisition system as the wars in Ukraine and Iran accelerate demand for rapid commercial innovation.
sections.whyItMatters: ICEYE's €2 billion bid for Avio illustrates Europe's push for sovereign space-launch capacity, even as Washington pushes back against European procurement rules that sideline US defense contractors.

sections.heading: Russian Tu-95 Bombers Touch Down in Vietnam After Japan Airspace Incursions; Siberian Crash Kills 19
sections.body:
The War Zone, USNI News, and The Independent — Two Russian Tu-95 strategic bombers and two Il-76 transport aircraft landed in Da Nang, Vietnam, following northeast Asian air defense alerts in which suspected Russian military aircraft violated Japanese territorial airspace twice northwest of Okinoshima, prompting Tokyo to scramble fighter jets (The War Zone, USNI News). Back in Russia, a military aircraft crashed in Siberia, killing all 19 personnel on board (The Independent).

In European security negotiations, Breaking Defense reported that Moscow is demanding Finland leave NATO as part of any Ukraine settlement, reflecting centuries of Russian border sensitivity toward Helsinki. Separately, Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda confirmed that US troop rotations in Lithuania will continue beyond the current nine-month deployment (Defense News).
sections.whyItMatters: Russian long-range bomber deployments into Vietnam after testing Japanese airspace demonstrate Moscow's determination to project military presence across the Indo-Pacific despite heavy losses in Ukraine.

sections.heading: Senators Call Ford-Class Steam Catapults a 'Non-Starter' as Pentagon Fails Ninth Straight Audit
sections.body:
USNI News, Defense News, and Breaking Defense — Senate Armed Services Committee Chairman Roger Wicker told Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao during Tuesday's confirmation hearing that the White House's proposal to abandon electromagnetic catapults and revert future Ford-class aircraft carriers to steam catapults is a 'non-starter' due to cost and technical risk (USNI News, The War Zone, Breaking Defense). Senators also pressed Cao over transparency to Congress, suicide mitigation policies, and his analogy comparing Navy shipboard food shortages (Defense News, The Hill).

Across the department, the Pentagon failed its ninth consecutive annual financial audit according to an inspector general report, though officials noted that a majority of defense units passed individual reviews for the first time (Defense News). Meanwhile, the White House formally nominated Gen. Christopher LaNeve to become Army Chief of Staff and Lt. Gen. Marcus Evans to serve as vice chief (Breaking Defense, Defense News).
sections.whyItMatters: Bipartisan Senate resistance to reverting Ford-class carriers to steam catapults underscores growing congressional pushback against costly White House hardware reversals amid the Pentagon's ninth audit failure.

sections.heading: Hanwha Fires Sea-Based Multi-Rocket Pod as US Army Launches Small-Drone Manufacturing Rodeo
sections.body:
Defense News and Breaking Defense — South Korean defense prime Hanwha successfully launched missiles at sea from a palletizable multi-pod rocket launcher, demonstrating a modular system capable of turning commercial or auxiliary vessels into floating rocket-artillery platforms (Defense News). In the United States, the Army kicked off a 'manufacturing rodeo' focused on small tactical drones ahead of its third Drone Dominance Gauntlet in March, where prototypes will face complex obstacles, heavy electronic jamming, and live target arrays (Breaking Defense).

At the same time, Army Undersecretary Michael Obadal warned that Army Aviation is suffering rising accident rates and falling year-over-year fully mission capable readiness (Breaking Defense). On the Ukraine battlefield, Defense News documented Kyiv's expanding use of large aerial drones to evacuate wounded soldiers from forward trenches to field hospitals, while Trump's push for nuclear arms cuts at the Shenzhen summit with Xi Jinping and Putin drew low expectations from defense observers.
sections.whyItMatters: Modular containerized sea-launchers from Hanwha and the US Army's anti-jamming drone gauntlet highlight how militaries are prioritizing expendable, distributed firepower and unmanned logistics.

sections.heading: Kuwait and Bahrain Intercept Aerial Attacks as Saudi Coalition Strikes 60 Houthi Targets
sections.body:
France 24, Anadolu Agency, and The Guardian — Kuwaiti air defenses engaged hostile drone attacks on Wednesday while Bahrain reported intercepting Iranian aerial strikes, keeping Gulf states on high alert after an American strike hit Iran's Qeshm Island (France 24). In Yemen, the Saudi-led coalition said it destroyed 60 Houthi targets to degrade ballistic missile and drone launch capabilities, while Yemen's military reported neutralizing 178 Houthi fighters across 660 operations (Anadolu Agency).

In defense counterintelligence and security, a US Army lieutenant colonel arrested in the United Kingdom on November 10 on suspicion of spying for Russia was transferred into US military custody (The Guardian), while a classified communications network at the National Security Agency suffered an outage (AP News). Elsewhere, Ecuadorian fishermen filed suit against the Trump administration over an allegedly unlawful drone strike launched from a US-operated vessel (Al Jazeera), and Irish prosecutors charged a 48-year-old man with damaging a parked US military C-130 transport aircraft (Al Jazeera).
sections.whyItMatters: Active air-defense engagements over Kuwait and Bahrain alongside counter-drone strikes in Yemen show Gulf air-defense stockpiles facing sustained real-world attrition.

bottomLine: Wednesday's defense picture highlights growing industrial and operational strain across every major theater: Finland's ICEYE bid €2 billion for Italy's Avio to bolster European space autonomy even as the Pentagon warned NATO against excluding US firms, Russian bombers deployed to Vietnam after violating Japanese airspace, senators shot down reverting Ford-class carriers to steam catapults, and Kuwait and Bahrain intercepted fresh Gulf aerial attacks.
